title: The Unerring Arrow Meets Its Match
story:
The war at Kurukshetra was over, and the Pandavas had won it — but victory had left Hastinapura a house of mourning, its sons fallen, its future in doubt. Krishna, who had guided them through the long conflict, was preparing to take his leave and return to Dwaraka when the cry came: a young woman running toward him across the palace courtyard, her hands clasped, her face white with terror.

"Protect me, protect me, great yogin, Lord of gods, master of the world!" she cried. "May this blazing iron-tipped arrow burn me, but let my embryo not fall."

She was Uttara, the daughter of King Virata, and the child in her womb was all that remained of the Pandavas' hopes. The war had won them a kingdom and cost them nearly everything else; the next generation of their house had been cut down in the terrible days after the fighting, and one unborn child now stood between the Kuru line and its end. It was to finish that last hope that Drona's son Ashvatthama had loosed his weapon — aimed, precisely, so that the Pandavas would be left without an heir.

And the arrow was already in the air, flying toward her. It was the Brahmashira, the supreme weapon of its age — unerring, they said, and beyond any counter, a thing no shield could stop and no wall turn. It sought its mark like a falcon and was not known to miss, and its mark now was a few hundred yards of palace air, and the small life at the end of them.

Krishna understood all of it in a moment. He was the indwelling soul of all beings, the lord of yoga; the weapon's intent was as plain to him as its flight, and the terror in the young woman's face moved him more than the fire in the sky. He reached for no bow and shouted no command. By his own maya he entered the womb of Virata's daughter and gathered the unborn child into his protection, and the Sudarshana disc blazed up around the small life within her — a ring of fire, patient and absolute, that no weapon could pass.

In the courtyard a hush fell; men held their breath, women turned their faces away, even the birds had stopped calling. The unerring arrow arrived — and found nothing to strike. Against that quiet ring of light the Brahmashira, the weapon that had never failed, the weapon armies had learned to fear at terrible cost, spent itself and died, quenched as a flame is quenched. Those who watched drew a breath and called it a wonder. And so it was. The verse adds, gently: do not be astonished, for all wonders have their home in him.

In time the child was born, whole and unharmed, and the Kuru line had its heir. He would be called Parikshit — the child of the womb that Krishna had entered and held. And Uttara, who had asked only that the child live, kept both her own life and his. The house that had been saved by a ring of light kept, in that small life, everything it had nearly lost.
reflection: Uttara's prayer is the whole story in one sentence: burn me, but let the child live. Krishna's answer is not to destroy the weapon but to stand inside the danger — protection here is presence, a lord of yoga wrapping himself around a life too small to defend itself.
hero_scene: Uttara running across the palace courtyard of Hastinapura toward Krishna, hands clasped in terror, while above her the blazing iron arrow of the Brahmashira streaks down from the sky — and Krishna stands calm as the Sudarshana disc encircles the child in her womb in a ring of light.

the blazing Brahmashira arrow streaking across the sky
Krishna standing calm in the courtyard
the Sudarshana disc glowing around the womb like a ring of fire
